I have opened a PR here:

https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/pull/35906

It introduces SimpleGraph.Walk.IsChord and SimpleGraph.Walk.IsChordless for closed walks in simple graphs, together with some basic API.

I would be very grateful for any reviews, comments, or suggestions.

Hello :wave:
Suggestion: heavily shorten your PR description. It seems unnecessarily long and I couldn't find useful information in it. Concretely, I suggest:

Add `Walk.IsChord` and `Walk.IsChordless` predicates in a new file `SimpleGraph/Walks/Chords.lean`.
See "chord" in https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_graph_theory

Thank you very much for the suggestion. I previously did not know what I should include in a PR description, so I added a lot of redundant information, which may indeed have made the review process less convenient.
Previously you mentioned that these new definitions are useful for reasoning about induced chordless cycles. Do you have an example theorem where these definitions make it easier?

Yes. A concrete example from my erdos751 project is the theorem
exists_chordless_cycle_of_exists_cycle in Erdos751/BV.lean:122, whose proof uses the auxiliary lemma shorter_cycle_of_chord in Erdos751/BV.lean:18.

Its proof uses the auxiliary lemma shorter_cycle_of_chord in Erdos751/BV.lean:18: if a cycle has a chord, then one can construct a strictly shorter cycle. Then, by choosing a shortest cycle, one concludes that it must be chordless.

So in that argument, IsChord is exactly the interface for the “extra ambient edge not belonging to the cycle” that lets me cut the cycle and produce a shorter one, and IsChordless is the natural final conclusion.

There is also a later use in BVDelta3_key_core in Erdos751/BV.lean:1290. In that proof, chordlessness is used at Erdos751/BV.lean:1322 to show that if two vertices of the cycle are adjacent in the ambient graph, then that edge must already belong to the cycle; otherwise it would be a chord.

So in my case these definitions are not only naming conveniences: they appear both in the shortest-cycle argument producing a chordless cycle and in later structural arguments about how the ambient graph interacts with that cycle.

Here is my erdos751 project github link

Ooh that sounds pretty cool, so basically the use is to define what a minimal cycle means, i.e.
p.IsChordless ↔ MinimalFor IsCycle ({ v | v ∈ ·.support }) p
I think these definitions shouldn't require the walk to be closed though, they sound useful for any walk

I am not entirely sure whether mathlib prefers notions that adhere strictly to the standard mathematical definition, or notions that are more broadly useful in practice. The definition of a chord that I learned is one for cycles. I think one could instead define a similar notion, perhaps called shortcut edge, as an analogue of the chord definition

tianyi zhao said:

I am not entirely sure whether mathlib prefers notions that adhere strictly to the standard mathematical definition, or notions that are more broadly useful in practice.

The second one, see #31690

I think there are two possible approaches: one is to broaden the definition of chord so that it can be applied to non-closed walks as well; the other is to define an additional notion analogous to a chord for non-closed walks, so that the closed and non-closed cases remain distinguished.
